Pathology of the Heart Part 3-5

Congenital Heart Disease · Cardiomyopathies · Myocarditis · COVID Heart · Valvular Disease · Pericarditis · Cardiac Neoplasms  |  LE 2 Trans 5C

Lecture at a Glance

This lecture covers the diseases that are neither ischemic nor hypertensive in origin: structural anomalies present at birth (congenital heart disease), intrinsic diseases of the heart muscle (cardiomyopathies, myocarditis, COVID heart disease), valvular heart disease, pericarditis, and cardiac neoplasms.

Learning objectives: understand definitions and apply knowledge related to causes, pathophysiology, morphology, clinical features, complications and prognosis of Congestive Heart Failure, Myocardial Diseases and Cardiomyopathies, Valvular Heart Failure and Pericardial Diseases.

Main Framework

Congenital Heart Disease (CHD)
  • Left to Right shunt → acyanotic at birth: ASD, VSD, AVSD, PDA
    • Pulmonary HTN after 2 to 3 decades → late cyanosis (Eisenmenger). Exception: AVSD has early cyanosis
  • Right to Left shunt → early cyanosis (blue babies): the "T's" — Tetralogy of Fallot, Transposition, Truncus arteriosus, Tricuspid atresia, TAPVR
  • Obstructive: Coarctation of aorta, Pulmonic stenosis/atresia, Aortic stenosis/atresia
Myocardial Disease
    • Cardiomyopathy (disease of exclusion): Dilated (weak, flabby)
    • Hypertrophic (muscle-bound)
    • Restrictive (stiff)
    • ARVC (fibro-fatty RV)
  • Myocarditis: inflammatory disease of the heart muscle
    • Viruses are the most common cause
  • COVID-19 heart disease: spike protein S binds ACE2. Cytokine storm → fulminant myocarditis
Valvular, Pericardial, Neoplastic
  • Valvular: degenerative calcification, infective endocarditis, NBTE, Libman-Sacks, carcinoid, rheumatic fever/RHD, mitral valve prolapse
  • Pericarditis: serous, fibrinous (most common), hemorrhagic, purulent, healed
  • Neoplasm: myxoma (adults), rhabdomyoma (children)

Must Know — Top Anchors of the Whole Lecture
  • VSD is the most common form of CHD (40% in infants)
    • Secundum ASD is 90% of ASD.
  • TOF is the most common R-L shunt
    • Pink tetralogy = mild PS, L-R, acyanotic
    • Classic tetralogy = severe PS, R-L, cyanotic.
  • DCMP: four negative criteria
    • HCMP: MYBP-C / β-MHC, leading cause of SCD in adolescents
    • RCMP: EMF most common, amyloidosis most common secondary
    • ARVC: RV aneurysms pathognomonic.
  • Myocarditis hallmark: focal myocyte necrosis surrounded by inflammatory cells
    • GCM: multinucleated giant cells = sine qua non.
  • Calcific aortic stenosis = most frequent valve abnormality
    • MVP = most common valvular disease in industrialized countries.
  • Fibrinous pericarditis = most common pericarditis ("bread and butter")
    • Myxoma = most common primary cardiac tumor in adults
    • Rhabdomyoma = in children.

I. Congenital Heart Disease

Definition p.1

  • Structural anomalies of heart and great vessels present at birth due to faulty embryogenesis.
  • Occurs usually at the first trimester, during 3rd to 8th week of AOG, when heart and great vessels are formed.
  • The most severe abnormalities are incompatible with intrauterine survival. Significant heart malformations are common among premature infants and stillborn.

A. Incidence p.2

  • Higher rates on males compared to females
    • Higher incidence among prematures and stillborn.
  • ASD and VSD are the most common CHD.
  • Most common: Atrial septal defects, Ventricular septal defects, Pulmonary stenosis.
  • Least common: Tricuspid atresia, with frequency of 1%.
  • With improving technology and surgical intervention, mortality rate has steadily declined within the past 2 decades.
High-Yield Recap — Top three most common CHD (from the lecture's review questions)
  • Ventricular septal defect: 42% (most common L → R shunt)
  • Atrial septal defect: 10%
  • Pulmonary stenosis: 8%

B. Common Clinical Presentation p.2

Depends on the underlying nature of the defect, the size and extent of the malformation, and the age of onset of symptoms. Some patients are asymptomatic. Some have catastrophic courses with heart failure and hypotension.

Signs and symptoms
  • Murmur
  • Cyanosis
  • Failure to thrive
  • Dyspnea
  • Tachypnea
  • Edema
  • Clubbing of digits (distal blunting and enlargement of the tips of fingers and toes)
  • Polycythemia (high hemoglobin levels)
  • Dysmorphic features (may indicate an underlying more serious genetic disease complex)
Long-term complications
  • CHF
  • Onset of Pulmonary Hypertension
  • Infective Endocarditis
Work-up
Work-up
Echocardiography and cardiac catheterization now permit a detailed understanding of disordered anatomy before cardiac surgery.

C. Etiology p.2-3

Genetic factors

  • Sporadic genetic abnormalities are the major known causes of CHD: single gene mutation, small chromosomal losses, additions or deletions of whole chromosomes leading to trisomies and monosomies.
  • Most patients have no identifiable genetic risks. Even in those that do, nature and severity of the defect is highly variable
    • Thus, environmental factors alone or in combination with genetic factors are increasingly implicated.

D. Classification Must Know p.3

Structural anomalies in CHD are categorized into three major categories according to the functional abnormalities:

  • Left to right shunt anomaly
  • Right to left shunt anomaly
  • Obstructive anomaly: characterized by obstruction or blockage in the flow of the blood.
Key Definition — Shunt
  • Shunt is an abnormal communication between chambers (e.g. VSD and ASD), or between blood vessels (e.g. PDA).
  • Abnormal channels permit blood flow across pressure gradients from different sides of the heart.

II. Left to Right Shunt Anomaly

General Principle Must Know p.3

  • Produces Acyanotic Heart Disease.
  • Blood is diverted from the left side of the heart to the right side.
    • Due to differentials of pressure gradients, the natural flow of blood is from the left ventricle (high-pressure chamber) into the right ventricle (low-pressure chamber).
  • Seen in VSD by a hole in interventricular septum, in ASD by a hole in the atrial septum, and in PDA through persistent functional communication between the aorta and pulmonary artery.
  • Four congenital diseases that produce a left to right shunt anomaly: Atrial Septal Defect, Ventricular Septal Defect, Patent Ductus Arteriosus, Atrio-ventricular Septal Defect.
Must Know — Common course of all L-R shunts
  • All L-R shunt anomalies will present as acyanotic at birth.
  • Pulmonary HTN can occur after 2 to 3 decades → late onset of cyanosis.
  • Exception: AVSD — early cyanosis.

A. Atrial Septal Defect (ASD)

Definition and Key Facts p.3

  • Abnormal opening in the atrial septum leading to direct communication between Left and Right atrium.
  • Communication between both atrial chambers allows blood to be diverted from left to right atrium.
    • Produces increased volume of blood flowing to the RA → RA volume overload.
    • Depending on the size of the defect and associated anomaly, this can result in a spectrum of disease ranging from no significant cardiac sequelae to right sided volume overload.
  • Associated complications: Pulmonary hypertension, Atrial arrhythmias.
  • Most common CHD that is asymptomatic until adulthood with symptoms appearing in the 3rd decade.
    • Often asymptomatic at birth and during childhood but may become progressively symptomatic in their 3rd-4th decade presenting with right ventricular failure.
  • Babies born with ASD are acyanotic at birth. Makes up approximately 10% of all congenital abnormalities of the heart.
  • Diagnosis of ASD is made on Transthoracic Echocardiography.

Hemodynamic Changes in ASD p.3-4

Hole or gap in the atrial septum → free communication between LA and RA
↓
LA has higher pressure than RA → blood shunted LA → RA (left to right shunting anomaly)
↓
Increased volume of blood flow to RA → RA volume overload → adaptive RA enlargement and dilatation → greater blood flow and volume overload in the RV
↓
Morphologic effects: right atrial dilatation and right ventricular hypertrophy. A diastolic murmur may occur due to increased blood flow across the pulmonary and tricuspid valves
↓
Increased blood flow to the right side → lungs produce increased pulmonary pressure → pulmonary hypertension
↓
When pulmonary HTN is severe enough and the pressure gradient overcomes the pressure in the RV → shunt reverses to right to left → cyanosis → Eisenmenger syndrome
Clinical Cue — Why no early cyanosis
  • Patients do not manifest cyanosis early because the blood that is shunted is largely oxygenated.
  • Blood to the right chamber is a mixture of deoxygenated blood from the venous circulation and oxygenated blood from the shunted left atrium.

Development of ASD p.4

  • Between the 4th and 7th week of fetal life, two distinct flaps of tissue develop to divide the common cavity into LA and RA:
    • Septum primum
    • Septum secundum — grows upwards from the atrioventricular ring
  • In fetal life, these act as flap valves allowing blood to flow from the RA directly to the LA.
  • When the pulmonary circulation is established, it closes and in most cases the two layers of the flaps fuse together.
  • In many children, these flaps do not fuse and form an opening known as patent foramen ovale. Defect in this area is the usual form of ASD.
  • Less common defects are found low in the interatrial septum, close to the atrioventricular ring → may be associated with abnormalities of the MV.
  • Other uncommon types are associated with defects in the development of the pulmonary veins or the coronary sinuses.

Types of ASD

Secundum ASD Must Know p.4

  • Relatively common
    • Represents 90% of ASD. A central defect.
  • Occurs from the failure of the septum secundum to develop in the region of fossa ovale.
    • Results in a communication between LA and RA, directly causing L-R shunt.
    • Results in volume overload of the right side of the heart and increased blood flow to the lungs.
  • Septum secundum: membranous ingrowth in the middle portion of the atrial septum that covers the ostium secundum, leaving only a small channel called the foramen ovale that is continuous with the ostium secundum.
    • Foramen ovale and ostium secundum permit continued R-L shunting of blood during intrauterine development.
    • The flap of septum secundum opens and closes in response to pressure gradients between LA and RA. This valve opens only when the pressure is greater in the RA.
Must Know — Fetal to postnatal pressure switch
  • In fetal life, the lungs are nonfunctional, and the pressure in the pulmonary circulation is greater than that of the systemic circulation
    • RA is under a higher pressure than the LA, and the valve of foramen ovale is normally open intrauterinely.
  • At birth, with lung expansion, the pulmonary vascular pressures drop, and the right atrial pressures fall below those in the LA. As a result, the valve of foramen ovale closes, and it usually becomes permanently sealed before adulthood.
  • When this persists, ASD can develop.

Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO) p.4-5

  • Tunnel-like space between the overlying septum secundum and septum primum.
  • Closes in 75% of people at birth when the septum primum and secundum fuse.
  • Closes permanently in approximately 80% of people by 2 years of age. In the remaining 20%, the unsealed flap can open if right-sided pressure becomes elevated.
  • In utero, the foramen ovale is necessary for the flow of blood across the fetal atrial septum.
  • Once pulmonary circulation is established after birth, LA pressure increases → functional closure → followed by anatomical closure of the septum primum and secundum by the age of 1 year.
  • In approximately 25% of people, a patent foramen ovale persists into adulthood.

Primum ASD p.5

  • Represents 5% of ASD.
  • The defect is low-lying, located near the Atrioventricular valve.
  • Often associated with structural abnormalities of the mitral valve and/or VSD.
  • Septum primum: crescent-shaped membranous ingrowth that sits posteriorly between the right and left atria and partially separates the chambers.
    • Ostium primum: transient, small anterior opening of septum primum, which allows movement of blood from the LA to the RA during early fetal development.
  • Persistence of ostium primum leads to a Primum ASD.

Sinus Venosus Defect p.5

  • Rare type of ASD. 5% of ASD.
  • Defect is high in the region of the entrance of superior vena cava.
  • Primarily associated with the sinus venosus, but can also be associated with IVC. Appear near SVC (more common) and IVC.
  • Typical malformation: interatrial communication caused by a deficiency of the common wall between the SVC and the right-side pulmonary veins.
  • Associated with Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return (TAPVR), which produces additional L-R shunting.

ASD Clinical Features and Effects p.5

Timing
Timing
Asymptomatic in the first 2 decades. Symptoms occur in the 3rd to 4th decade of life due to development of pulmonary hypertension.
Signs and symptoms
Signs and symptoms
Dyspnea, fatigue, edema, palpitations, arrhythmia, shortness of breath, murmur (caused by high blood flow towards the Pulmonary valve)
Complications
Complications
Stroke, Pulmonary Hypertension, Eisenmenger complex (produces reversal of the shunt)

Effects of ASD

  • RA hypertrophy and enlargement and RV hypertrophy and enlargement — both are reflections of adaptive responses to the increased volume overload.
  • Increased pulmonary blood flow → eventually produces pulmonary hypertension.
  • Murmur due to increased blood flow to the pulmonary valve → clinically a diastolic murmur can be elicited.
  • Right sided heart failure.
High-Yield Recap — ASD types (lecture summary)
  • Secundum ASD — area of fossa ovale (90%)
  • Primum ASD — near atrioventricular valve (low lying, 5%)
  • Sinus venosus defect — near SVC (high lying, 5%)
  • Effects: RVH, RAH, pulmonary HTN, murmurs

B. Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)

Definition and Key Facts Must Know p.5-6

  • Defect in the septum that divides the RV and LV. Communication between the two ventricular chambers allows blood to be shunted from the left side to the right side of the heart.
  • Most common form of CHD, accounting for 40% of cases in infants.
  • Associated with fetal alcohol syndrome.
  • A minority (about 30%) occur as an isolated anomaly. Majority are complexed with other CHD like tetralogy of Fallot.
  • Classified as L-R shunt anomaly → acyanotic at birth.
  • Small defects in the muscular wall may spontaneously close in 50% of cases as the patient ages, especially with muscular VSD.
  • Surgical closure is an indication for larger membranous and muscular defects.
  • The size and site of the defect determines the extent of the shunt
    • Defects on the membranous septum may be associated with valvular abnormalities, particularly aortic incompetence.

Hemodynamics of VSD p.6

Defect or hole in the interventricular septum → communication between LV and RV
↓
Unidirectional flow from left side (high pressure) to right side (low pressure) → left to right shunt
↓
Increased blood flow from LV to RV → volume overload to the right side of the heart and the lungs
↓
Long term effect: RV hypertrophy, RA dilatation, pulmonary HTN
Must Know This allows mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood so patients with VSD have no cyanosis.

Types of VSD (classified by location of the defect) p.6

The ventricular septum consists of an inferior muscular and superior membranous portion.

TypeFrequencyLocation and notes
Membranous VSD90% of VSD cases
  • Located in the region of the membranous interventricular septum.
  • Majority measure 2 to 3 cm in diameter.
  • It is the most common type of VSD.
Infundibular VSD10% of VSD casesOccurs below the pulmonary valve.
Muscular VSD—
  • Located within the muscular wall of the interventricular septum.
  • 50% of muscular VSD generally close spontaneously.

Clinical Features of VSD p.6

  • Usually asymptomatic and acyanotic at birth.
  • Symptoms appear earlier in the pediatric age group (in contrast with ASD).
  • Associated with other congenital cardiac anomalies such as TOF. Only 20-30% are isolated anomalies.
  • Functional consequences depend on the size of the defect and associated malformations
    • Spontaneous regression in 50% of muscular VSD.
  • Large defects are usually membranous or infundibular and have earlier RVH and pulmonary HTN. Large defects may lead to an Eisenmenger complex.
  • Signs and symptoms: Tachypnea, Dyspnea, Fatigue, Failure to thrive.
Must Know — Diagnostic physical finding Loud pansystolic murmur with a thrill — a diagnostic physical finding of VSD, often with associated thrill.
Must Know — Complications
  • CHF (most important complication)
  • Infective endocarditis

C. Atrioventricular Septal Defect (AVSD)

Definition Must Know p.7

  • AKA endocardial cushion defect or atrioventricular canal defect.
  • Anatomic defect that arises from the faulty development of the embryonic endocardial cushions, which represent the primordia of the atrioventricular septum and atrioventricular valves.
Must Know
  • Results in an incomplete closure of the atrioventricular septum and inadequate formation of the TV and MV.
  • Primary defect: failure of the formation of the part of the heart that arises from embryonic structures called the endocardial cushions.

Endocardial cushions

  • Responsible for separating the central parts of the heart near the TV and MV (atrioventricular valves), which separate the atria from the ventricles.
  • Complete the separation of the MV and TV by dividing the single valve between the embryonic atria and ventricles.
  • Structures that develop from the endocardial cushions:
    • lower part of the atrial septum
    • higher portion of the ventricular septum
    • atrioventricular valves.
Abnormal passageway between the two sides → blood from both sides mixes
→
Too much blood circulates back to the lungs before it travels through the body
→
Pulmonary HTN → Eisenmenger's syndrome and cyanosis
  • Accounts for 5% of CHD. Most common among infants with Down's syndrome (about 15-20% of newborns with Down syndrome have AVSD).

Types of AVSD p.7

Partial AVSDComplete AVSD
  • The defect is primarily in the atrial septum and the mitral valve.
  • The part of the ventricular septum formed by the endocardial cushion has been filled in (by tissue from AV valves or from endocardial cushion tissue), and the TV and MV are divided into two distinct valves.
  • Produces the ostium primum type of ASD and is usually associated with a cleft in the mitral valve that may cause the valve to leak.
  • Large combined AVSD, common in mitral valve and tricuspid valve.
  • Defects in all structures formed around the endocardial cushion: atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, and defects in the atrioventricular valve.
  • All four chambers are freely communicating with each other.
Clinical Cue — Why complete AVSD is worse
  • A much bigger L-R shunt with all four chambers freely communicating → greater volume shunted to the right → earlier RVH, more pronounced RA dilatation, increased pulmonary blood flow.
  • Pulmonary hypertension and the Eisenmenger complex occur much earlier, so patients will have more symptoms.

D. Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA)

Definition and Development p.7-8

  • Communication between two great vessels, aorta and pulmonary artery, through a persistent and functioning ductus arteriosus.
  • In normal embryonic development, the ductus arteriosus arises from the pulmonary artery and joins the aorta just distal to the origin of the left subclavian artery.
  • During intrauterine life, it permits blood flow from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, thereby bypassing the unoxygenated lungs.
  • Shortly after birth in healthy term infants, the ductus constricts and is functionally closed after 1-2 days. This occurs in response to:
    • Increased oxygen tension
    • Decreased pulmonary vascular resistance
    • Declining local level of prostaglandin E2
  • Majority are related to an isolated anomaly.
Key Threshold A persistent ductus arteriosus is diagnosed when the ductus arteriosus fails to close after 72 hours.

Effects of PDA p.8

  • A patent ductus allows blood to be shunted from the aorta (left side) to the right side of the venous system in the direction of the pulmonary artery.
  • PDA increases the pulmonary blood flow and left atrial and ventricular volumes.
  • PDAs account for ~7% of cases of CHD: 90% isolated anomaly, 10% associated with other defects such as VSD, coarctation of the aorta, pulmonic or aortic valvular stenosis.
  • Physiologic consequences depend on the ductal size: a small ductus causes minimal symptoms, a large ductus causes a large left to right shunt.
  • Over time, the large shunt results in: Left ventricular enlargement → Pulmonary artery hypertension → Elevated vascular resistance → ultimately Eisenmenger syndrome.
  • Morphologic effects: Right ventricular hypertrophy, Right atrial dilatation, Long standing pulmonary hypertension.
Must Know — Characteristic murmur PDA produces a characteristic continuous murmur, which we call a machinery type of murmur (continuous, harsh, "machinery-like").

Clinical Features of PDA p.8

  • Depend on the size of the ductus and how much blood flow it carries.
  • Acyanotic at birth. When symptomatic: Tachypnea, Dyspnea, Fatigue, Failure to thrive.
  • Complications: CHF, Infective endocarditis, Pulmonary HPN.
High-Yield Recap — Left-to-Right Shunt Anomalies (lecture summary)
  • ASD:
    • Secundum (fossa ovale)
    • Primum (near AV valve, low lying)
    • Sinus venosus (near SVC, high lying)
      • Effects: RVH, RAH, pulmonary HTN, murmurs.
  • VSD:
    • Membranous (membranous septum)
    • Infundibular (below the PV)
    • Muscular (muscular wall).
  • AVSD:
    • Partial (atrial septum and MV → ostium primum ASD with cleft MV, leaky valve)
    • Complete (all structures around the endocardial cushions → all four chambers freely communicating).
  • PDA: persistence of functional communication between pulmonary artery and aorta → continuous harsh "machinery-like" murmur.
  • All L-R shunt anomalies present as acyanotic at birth. Pulmonary HTN after 2 to 3 decades → late cyanosis
    • Exception: AVSD — early cyanosis.

III. Right to Left Shunt Anomaly

General Principle Must Know p.9

  • AKA cyanotic congenital heart disease. Group of CHDs that cause cyanosis early in the postnatal life.
  • Occurs when deoxygenated blood from the right side flows directly into the left side of the heart bypassing the pulmonary circulation, resulting in hypoxemia and cyanosis.
    • Poorly oxygenated blood shunts directly into the systemic arterial circulation. Hence, cyanosis is an important clinical presentation.
  • Early cyanosis: symptom of R-L shunt.
R-L shunt
→
↓ blood flow through the pulmonary system
→
↓ blood O2 levels and hypoxemia (cyanosis)
→
Blue babies at birth
The 5 CHDs in this category — all "T's"
  • Tetralogy of Fallot (most common)
  • Transposition of Great Vessels
  • Truncus Arteriosus
  • Tricuspid Atresia
  • Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return

A. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)

Four Cardinal Features Must Know p.9

A type of cyanotic heart disease producing a R-L shunting anomaly. Manifests with early cyanosis at birth. Most common form of R-L shunt heart disease.

ComponentWhat it does
1. VSDAllows blood to be shunted from the R to L side of the heart because blood cannot go to the pulmonary artery due to pulmonary artery obstruction.
2. Subpulmonic stenosis
  • Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract due to the presence of a subpulmonic stenosis
  • Does not allow blood to go to the pulmonary artery for oxygenation and may lead to severe hypoxemia.
3. Aorta overriding the VSDAorta is misplaced and moves toward the right side over the VSD. The positioning of the great vessels is arrested midway because of the failure of development of the membranous portion of aorta.
4. Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH)Adaptive response caused by inability of blood to go to the pulmonary artery due to pulmonary stenosis.

All of these components result embryologically from the anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum.

Development and Pathophysiology p.9-10

  • During fetal life, the infundibulum does not rotate to its normal anatomic location with the developmental arrest of the septum at the mid portion → produces an aorta located beneath the overriding interventricular septum.
  • Concomitant failure in the formation of the membranous septum → a defect (VSD).
  • In the infundibulum, the pulmonary artery development is affected and is wedged and pressed → subaortic stenosis. As a result of the greater workload against an obstructed pulmonary outflow tract, the RV adapts by RV hypertrophy.
  • Blood is shunted from the R side to the L side via the opening of the VSD and the outflow tract obstruction at the stenotic pulmonary artery.
Must Know — Most important determinant of severity
  • Most important determinant of the severity and clinical consequences of TOF: degree of RV outflow obstruction due to pulmonary stenosis.
  • Lesser obstruction → blood is shunted from L to R and permitted to preferentially enter the pulmonary circulation, allowing oxygenation.
  • Greater degree of obstruction → blood is forced away from the pulmonary circuit leftward towards the VSD, hence flow is from R to L.
Venous blood → R atrium → R ventricle
↓
Pulmonary stenosis → outflow tract obstruction impeding blood flow to the lungs, preventing oxygenation
↓
Blood shunted R ventricle → L ventricle via the VSD, bypassing the lungs
↓
Cyanosis manifests early at birth. RV hypertrophy comes in to overcome the pressure gradient against the obstructed pulmonary outflow tract

Morphology of TOF Must Know p.10

  • Heart enlargement — classically "boot-shaped" due to the marked RVH.
  • Large VSD and displacement of the aorta and aortic valves at the superior border, thereby overriding the VSD.
    • Aortic valve is enlarged and appears to arise from both the L and R ventricles instead of the L ventricle as in the normal heart.
  • The obstruction to RV outflow is most often due to the narrowing of the infundibulum (subaortic stenosis) but can also be accompanied by pulmonary valvular stenosis
    • Sometimes, complete atresia of the pulmonary valve can be identified.
  • Other accompanying lesions: the presence of a PDA may be necessary for survival. Aortic valve insufficiency or an ASD may also be present.

Clinical Features of TOF p.10

  • Clinical features and survival of TOF depend on the severity of subpulmonic stenosis.
  • Most infants with TOF are cyanotic at birth and soon thereafter.
  • The more severe the pulmonic stenosis = the more hypoplastic the pulmonary arteries = the larger the overriding aorta.
  • Shunting of oxygen-poor blood → reduction in arterial oxygen saturation → babies appear cyanotic or blue.
  • Systolic murmurs are present and can result either from a VSD or from pulmonary stenosis.
  • Other signs and symptoms:
    • Hypoxic patients: ↑ Hgb concentration → polycythemia.
    • Characteristic squatting posture with a "seat-in-a-knee chest" position — may be an attempt to ↑ venous return from the lower limbs.
    • Rapid breathing in response to ↓ O2 tension.
  • Complications: RV failure, Infective Endocarditis.
Pink TetralogyClassic Tetralogy of Fallot
Mild pulmonary stenosisSevere pulmonary stenosis
L-R shuntR-L shunt
Without cyanosis (acyanotic babies) — resembles an isolated VSDWith cyanosis (cyanotic babies) — R sided pressure approaches or exceeds left sided pressure

B. Transposition of Great Vessels (TOGV)

Key Facts p.10-11

  • AKA transposition of the great arteries. Produces ventriculo-arterial discordance.
  • In the more common variant, the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery emanates from the LV.
    • Allows blood from the venous circulation to be shunted directly to the systemic circulation via the malpositioned aorta arising in the RV → right-to-left shunt anomaly.
  • Cyanosis develops early because blood fails to reach the pulmonary circulation
    • This is incompatible with life.
  • Without arterial switch surgery, most patients die within days or months.
Associated lesions
  • VSD and PDA — may be lifesaving as they allow blood to enter the pulmonary circulation for oxygenation.
  • RVH — RV becomes hypertrophic as it needs higher workload to propel blood to the systemic circulation.
  • LV hypoplasia — the LV becomes thin-walled (atrophic) as it supports the low-resistance pulmonary circulation.

C. Truncus Arteriosus

Key Facts p.11

  • Uncommon congenital CV anomaly characterized by a single arterial trunk arising from the normally formed ventricles by means of a single semilunar valve known as a truncal valve.
  • Caused by the failure of separation of the great vessels (aorta and PA) → single large vessel (truncus arteriosus).
  • This great vessel usually has 1 large valve which may have 2-5 leaflets and usually sits over both the LV and RV. Associated VSD can be seen
    • The single artery originates from the heart above a VSD.
  • Presents with cyanosis in the first few days of life. Excessive blood flow to the lungs → CHF in the first few weeks of life. Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly.

D. Tricuspid Atresia

Key Facts p.11

  • Complete absence of the TV (tricuspid valve)
    • Absence of right AV connection leads to hypoplastic, undersized or absent RV.
  • Results embryologically from unequal division of the AV canal: MV larger than normal, RV underdeveloped and hypoplastic.
  • Blood from venous circulation can enter the RA, but because of the complete absence of the TV, blood cannot enter the RV. Blood can enter the L side only in presence of ASD. Circulation is maintained by R-L shunting through an interatrial communication (ASD or patent foramen ovale).
  • Cyanosis is present from birth. High early mortality.
  • Signs and symptoms depend on the presence and size of the VSD and the relationship of the great arteries.
Must Know — Both an ASD and a VSD must be present An ASD and VSD must both be present to maintain blood flow from right to left, to allow access to the lungs.
RA
→
ASD
→
LA
→
LV
→
VSD
→
RV
→
Lungs

E. Total Anomalous Pulmonary Venous Return (TAPVR)

Key Facts p.11-12

  • The PV are the 4 blood vessels (2 on each side) that return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the L atrium.
  • TAPVR is a rare congenital malformation in which all 4 PVs do not connect normally into the LA. Instead they drain abnormally to the RA by way of an anomalous connection (into the coronary sinus or left innominate veins).
  • Associated lesions: ASD, PDA.
  • Morphologic effects: RAD (right atrial dilatation), RVH, Pulmonary trunk dilatation, Hypoplastic LA.
Abnormal pulmonary vein connection → oxygenated blood returning from the lungs mixes with the deoxygenated blood from the venous circulation
↓
L side of the heart is filled only by mixed blood shunting across an ASD → ↓ overall oxygen content → explains cyanosis in TAPVR
↓
If the ASD is small or restrictive → ↓ volume of blood filling the LA and LV → may lead to low cardiac output and shock
High-Yield Recap — Right-to-Left Shunt Anomalies (lecture summary)
  • R-L shunt anomalies: all "T's".
  • TOF — most common R-L shunt
    • Anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular septum
    • VSD + RV outflow obstruction (subpulmonic stenosis, defines clinical presentation and survival) + overriding aorta + RVH. Boot-shaped RVH. Pink tetralogy (mild PS, L-R, acyanotic) vs Classic tetralogy (severe PS, R-L, cyanotic).
  • TOGV — aorta from RV, PA from LV. Incompatible with life unless associated with other CHD.
  • Truncus arteriosus — failure to separate into aorta and PA. Early cyanosis and pulmonary HTN due to mixing of blood.
  • Tricuspid atresia — complete absence of TV, large MV compensating
    • ASD and VSD both required: RA → ASD → LA → LV → VSD → RV → Lungs.
  • TAPVR — pulmonary veins do not drain into the LA, they drain into the coronary sinus or left innominate veins.

IV. Obstructive Anomaly

Congenital obstruction to blood flow can occur at the level of the heart valves or within a great vessel. Common examples: Coarctation of aorta, Pulmonic stenosis/atresia, Aortic stenosis/atresia.

A. Coarctation of Aorta (COA)

Definition and Types Must Know p.12

  • CHD wherein there is a localized constriction or stricture in a segment of the aorta → resulting in impedance to blood flow.
  • Accounts for up to 5% of all forms of congenital CV disease and is 2x more common in males.
  • May occur as an isolated defect or in association with other lesions, most commonly bicuspid aortic valve and VSD.
Infantile (Preductal) COAAdult (Postductal) COA
  • Coarctation/Tubular hypoplasia of aortic arch proximal to PDA. Usually symptomatic early.
  • Circumferential narrowing of the aortic segment between the L subclavian artery and the ductus arteriosus.
  • Ductus: typically patent
    • Main source of deoxygenated blood delivered to the distal aorta.
  • Pulmonary trunk: dilated due to ↑ blood flow because the R side of the heart now perfuses the body distal to the narrowed segment.
  • RV: hypertrophied.
  • Ridge-like coarctation at the level or after the PDA.
  • About 98% of coarctations are postductal (adult in nature), where the narrowing occurs distal to the ductus arteriosus.
  • Aorta is sharply constricted by a tissue ridge adjacent to the ductus arteriosus
    • Constricted segment: made up of smooth muscle and elastic fibers derived from the aortic media.
  • Proximal to the coarctation, the aortic arch and its branch vessels are dilated and the LV is hypertrophied.

Clinical Features of COA p.13

  • Signs and symptoms are largely dependent on the degree of constriction. If severe, symptoms develop soon after birth.
  • If undetected or untreated, a collateral circulation develops to ↑ blood flow to the lower part of the body — involves branches of the intercostal arteries, which become dilated and tortuous.
  • Abnormal blood flow through the coarcted segment may produce a systolic murmur, best heard in the posterior chest.
Must Know — Most characteristic clinical finding
  • HTN in the upper limbs, with a much lower pressure in vessels distal to the coarctation.
  • Femoral pulse: often reduced.

B. Pulmonic Stenosis/Atresia

Key Facts p.13

  • Relatively frequent malformation leading to obstruction at the level of the PV (pulmonary valve).
  • Obstruction may be mild to severe
    • Lesions can be isolated or part of a more complex anomaly, either TOF or TOGV.
  • RVH typically develops.
  • With coexistent subpulmonic stenosis (as in TOF), the pulmonary trunk is not dilated and may be hypoplastic.
  • When the valve is entirely atretic, there is no communication between the RV and lungs → associated with a hypoplastic RV and ASD. ASD may be necessary to allow blood from the R side to reach the lungs (may be via PDA as well).
  • Mild stenosis may be asymptomatic and compatible with long life
    • Symptomatic cases require surgical correction. When the RV is severely hypoplastic, blood can be surgically routed directly from the vena cava to the pulmonary artery, bypassing the right side of the heart.
  • Associated lesions: RVH, PA hypoplasia, ASD, RV hypoplasia, PV atresia.
High-Yield Recap — Obstructive Anomalies (lecture summary)
  • Infantile (Preductal):
    • before or proximal to PDA
    • tubular hypoplasia of aortic arch
    • narrowing between the left subclavian artery and the ductus arteriosus
    • pulmonary trunk dilated
    • RVH.
  • Adult (Postductal):
    • at the level or after the PDA
    • ridgelike coarctation
    • aorta sharply constricted by a tissue ridge adjacent to the ductus arteriosus
    • aortic arch and its branches dilated
    • LVH.
  • Characteristic clinical finding: HTN in the upper limbs, lower pressure in vessels distal to the coarctation.
  • Pulmonary stenosis/atresia: obstruction at the level of the PV.

V. Myocardial Disease

Intrinsic diseases primarily involving the heart muscles: inflammatory disorders (myocarditis), immunologic and systemic metabolic disorders, genetic abnormalities in cardiac muscle cells including cardiomyopathies.

A. Cardiomyopathies — Definition and Classification

Definition Must Know p.14

  • Heart disease resulting from a primary abnormality in the myocardium. Literally "cardiac muscle disease".
  • Characterized by cardiac dysfunction in which the main abnormality lies intrinsically within the myocardium. Expressed as diastolic and/or systolic ventricular dysfunction.
  • May affect one or both ventricles in a diffuse or multifocal fashion producing myocardial failure, arrhythmias, or sudden cardiac death.
  • Either confined to the heart or part of a generalized systemic disorder, often leading to cardiovascular death or progressive congestive heart failure.
Key Concept — Disease of exclusion
  • Known as a diagnosis of exclusion: excluding diseases of myocardium due to ischemic heart disease, myocarditis, hypertensive heart disease and valvular heart disease.
  • Another cause of primary cardiac muscle problem due to ischemia must be excluded.

Primary Cardiomyopathy

Idiopathic or heart muscle disease of unknown causes, which includes: Dilated, Hypertrophic, some Restrictive cardiomyopathy.

Secondary Cardiomyopathy

Heart muscle disease of known cause or associated with disorders of other systems. Attributed to: post-inflammatory, metabolic, toxic, infiltrative, physical agents, neuromuscular disorders, hematologic, immunologically-mediated.

Functional Classification p.14

Categorized based on the functional and morphological presentation:

TypeLecture descriptorCore dysfunction
Dilated CMPWeak-Flabby ("congestive")Global dilatation of all 4 chambers → hypocontracting, systolic dysfunction, low EF, low CO
Hypertrophic CMPMuscle-Bound
  • Asymmetrical septal hypertrophy
  • LV outflow obstruction
  • diastolic dysfunction
  • normal or increased EF
Restrictive CMPStiffInfiltrative substances (amyloid, iron, fibroelastic tissue) restricting movement → diastolic dysfunction
Arrhythmogenic RV dysplasia/CMP (ARVC)Newly added to WHO classificationReplacement of RV by fibro-fatty tissue → life-threatening arrhythmias and SCD

Dilated (Congestive) Cardiomyopathy (DCMP)

Key Facts Must Know p.14

  • Dilated Cardiomyopathy: Weak-Flabby. Known as congestive cardiomyopathy.
  • Most common type of cardiomyopathy: 90% of cardiomyopathies. Among the common causes of heart failure.
  • 25-35% have familial or genetic form.
  • Progressive global dilatation and hypertrophy → hypocontracting heart with significant reduction in LV ejection fraction and decreased cardiac output.
    • Contractile, systolic dysfunction
    • Low LV ejection fraction, low CO
    • Patients usually progress to CHF and arrhythmia
  • Cardiac abnormality: global enlargement and dilatation of all 4 chambers leading to a weak, flabby, hypocontracting heart with systolic dysfunction, usually with concomitant hypertrophy.
  • Patient often presents with congestive heart failure, hence the alternate name.
  • From a pathologic standpoint, the term DCMP designates an idiopathic process in the absence of long standing hypertension, toxic exposure to the heart or chronic alcoholism.

Epidemiology p.14-15

  • Estimated prevalence 1:2500.
  • Commonly occurs in the third or fourth decade of life
    • Most patients are middle aged or older at onset of symptoms.
  • Younger patients with DCMP often have a familial history and a genetic predisposition.

Causes p.15

DCMP by underlying etiology
  • Primary without family history or idiopathic — AKA sporadic dilated CMP. In most cases, no underlying identified etiology.
  • Secondary — associated with:
    • Previous viral myocarditis (15%) → leads to scarring and heart failure. Viruses implicated: Coxsackievirus, Adenovirus, Parvovirus
      • Non-inflammatory etiologies: Alcohol abuse (most prevalent toxic cause)
      • Pregnancy
      • Malnutrition
      • Drugs: Adriamycin therapy – dose related
      • Metals: cobalt, arsenic, lead, mercury
      • Autoimmune
  • Familial/Genetic — autosomal dominant/recessive/X-linked mutations, recessive mitochondrial defects in cytoskeleton or dystrophin gene (25%)
    • Single gene mutation involving the structural proteins: dystrophin, metavinculin, lamin and beta-mitochondrial DNA
    • Responsible for at least 25% of DCMP cases arising from an autosomal dominant form, primarily caused by a single mutation in genes including the cytoskeletal protein
    • Less commonly: mutations involving proteins of the sarcomere, nuclear membrane, and intercalated discs of myofibrils
    • Most common identifiable mutations: LMNA gene encoding the Lamin A and C nuclear envelope protein → these patients most commonly present with an atrioventricular block
Must Know — Four Negative Criteria (DCMP is a disease of exclusion)
  • No major coronary artery disease/anomaly
  • No valvular disease or anomaly
  • No systemic hypertension
  • No shunts within or outside the heart
  • Before DCMP can be diagnosed these structural abnormalities must first be excluded.

Morphology — Gross Must Know p.15-16

  • Increased weight and size — weighing 2-3x more than its normal weight.
  • Global enlargement — flabby with dilatation of all 4 chambers.
    • Cardiomegaly is usually considered a requisite for the diagnosis of DCMP.
  • Generalized chamber dilatation — there may be accompanying thinning of the cardiac wall
    • In most cases the thickness of ventricular wall is often normal, which contrasts with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
  • Valvular dilatation → functional regurgitation
    • No primary valvular structural alterations.
    • Mitral or tricuspid regurgitation results from marked chamber dilatation and widening of the valvular annulus — known as functional regurgitation. May also result from papillary muscle dysfunction secondary to ventricular dilatation and changes in ventricular wall shape.
    • Coronary arteries are usually free of significant narrowing
      • Any obstruction present is insufficient to explain the degree of cardiac dysfunction.
  • Associated changes
    • Mural thrombus — common. Source of pulmonary embolism when thrombi are on the right side.
    • Systemic thromboembolism — when the thromboembolic material is on the left side.
    • Ventricular endothelial/endocardial fibrous plaques — sequelae to thrombosis, in about 10% of cases.
    • Mild, diffuse, patchy endocardial fibrosis especially towards the ventricular outflow tract — likely a result of cardiac dilatation.

Morphology — Microscopic Must Know p.16

  • Myocardial hypertrophy with nuclear enlargement
  • Myofiber loss or attenuation — marked variation of myofiber size with hypertrophied muscles alternating with attenuated muscles, which are stretched and irregular in shape
  • Interstitial endocardial fibrosis
  • Important finding of DCMP: Polyploidy nuclei — lobated, hyperchromatic, highly distorted nuclei sometimes called "ninja star-like" nuclei
    • Although non-specific, when present in 55% of cases they are highly suggestive of titin truncation mutation
  • Negative findings important in the diagnosis: lack of inflammation, lack of amyloid or iron depositions and granuloma

Clinical Features and Prognosis p.16

  • Slowly progressive onset of symptoms of Congestive Heart Failure: shortness of breath, easy fatigability, orthopnea, dyspnea, edema, poor exertional capacity.
  • End stage patients: low ejection fraction of <25% (Normal: 50-65%), low cardiac output.
  • Secondary MV and TV regurgitation murmurs (secondary functional regurgitation).
  • Arrhythmia — ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias and conduction system abnormalities are common.
  • Thrombo-embolic complication — embolism from dislodgement of an intracardiac thrombus may occur.
  • Cardiac transplantation is frequently recommended.
Poor Prognosis — values
  • 50% of patients will die within 3 years (2 years per 2026 trans) upon diagnosis.
  • Only 25% will survive longer than 5 years.
  • Death is usually attributed to progressive cardiac failure or arrhythmia.

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCMP)

Key Facts Must Know p.16-17

  • Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Muscle-Bound.
  • AKA: IHSS (idiopathic hypertrophic subaortic stenosis), Hypertrophic Obstructive CMP (HOCMP), Asymmetrical Septal Hypertrophy.
  • Characterized by a heart that shows myometrial hypertrophy, abnormal diastolic filling and intermittent outflow tract obstruction in ⅓ of cases.
  • Heart is thick walled, heavy, and hypercontracting.
  • Primarily causes diastolic dysfunction with a usual preserved systolic function.
  • Salient morphological characteristics: asymmetrical myocardial hypertrophy, septal hypertrophy, LV outflow obstruction and abnormal diastolic filling.
  • Hypertrophy is NOT associated with ventricular dilatation. Increased or normal LV ejection fraction.
Must Know — The hallmark of the disorder
  • Presence of myocardial hypertrophy that is inappropriate, often asymmetrical and recurring in the absence of inciting hypertrophic stimulus.
  • This hypertrophy frequently involves the interventricular septum → obstruction of flow from the left ventricle outflow tract to the aorta → abnormal diastolic filling.
Must Know — "Banana-like" configuration
  • The disproportionate thickness of the interventricular septum (AKA asymmetrical septal hypertrophy) and free wall of the LV causes the bulging of the interventricular septum into the left ventricle forming the so-called "banana-like" configuration of the left ventricle.
  • This produces a heavy, muscular, hypercontracting heart with increased or normal LV ejection fraction and cardiac output.

Etiology and Pathogenesis Must Know p.17

  • Most cases are familial, transmitted as autosomal dominant in 60% of cases → 12 sarcomeric genes: β-HMC gene.
  • Caused by a mutation in any one of several genes that encode proteins that are part of the sarcomere, the contractile unit of cardiac myocytes and skeletal muscle.
    • Myosin-binding protein C (MYBP-C) or β-myosin heavy chain (β-MHC/MYH7)
    • Also actin, tropomyosin, and titin. Cardiac TnI, TnT, and α-tropomyosin.
    • Accounts overall for 70-80% of cases of HCMP.
    • These known genes are concerned with myofibril organization within the myocytes → disorganization leads to misshapen myocytes running in disordered rows and arrays.
  • Prognosis varies widely and correlates strongly with specific mutations.
    • Sarcomere mutations give rise to a defective energy transfer from the mitochondria (source of generation) to the sarcomere (site of use).
    • In contradistinction with DCMP: abnormality is seen in the cytoskeletal proteins → abnormality in contraction, force generation, force transmission or myocyte signaling.
  • All the genes carry a risk of a sudden unexpected death. Patients with some mutations, such as specific tropomyosin substitutions, have only mild ventricular hypertrophy with little or no LV outflow obstruction, but still carry a disproportionately high risk of sudden death.
Must Know HCMP is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in pre-adolescent or adolescent children.

Epidemiology p.17

  • Low overall prevalence: 0.05 - 0.2% of the general population
    • Incidence rate: 0.3 to 0.5 per 100,000.
  • Occurs in all ethnic groups and equally in both sexes.
  • Bimodal peak of occurrence, at the second and third decade of life, but may present at any age.
    • Children: inherited cases found from newborn to adulthood. Peak incidence: 2nd decade.
    • Adults: vast majority occur between the 3rd and 6th decades
      • Peak incidence: 3rd decade.

Morphology — Gross Must Know p.17-18

  • Massive LV myocardial thickening and hypertrophy without ventricular dilatation.
  • Pronounced asymmetrical septal hypertrophy with marked thickening of the interventricular septum.
    • Excessive enlargement of the septum compared to the LV wall → septal:wall ratio of >1.3.
    • Marked hypertrophy may include the entire septum, but it is mostly prominent in the subaortic region producing a LV outflow tract obstruction → associated with secondary fibrous endocardial plaque and thickening of the anterior mitral valve leaflets → elicits a systolic outflow murmur.
  • Banana-like ventricular cavity — on longitudinal sectioning, the normally round/ovoid LV cavity is compressed into a banana-like configuration due to the bulging of the septum into the lumen.
  • Secondary changes: +/- endocardial thickening, mural plaque thickening, anterior mitral valve thickening.
Values — septal/posterior wall thickness ratio in adults >1.3 in normotensive patients >1.5 in hypertensive patients

Morphology — Microscopic Must Know p.18

  • Extensive myocyte hypertrophy — hypertrophied with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and box-shaped nuclei. Display bizarre forms with Y-shaped branching, frequent side-to-side junctions, or a characteristic whorled appearance around a central fibrous core.
  • Haphazard myocardial fiber disarray — disorganized bundles of cardiomyocytes arranged at perpendicular and oblique angles to each other.
    • Normal myocyte arrangement: sweeping fascicles in one direction.
    • In HCMP: irregular disarray with parallel orientation and whorling pattern.
    • Myocardial disarray is specific for HCMP when it is diffuse or when it involves at least 20% of one or more tissue blocks.
  • Interstitial fibrosis — resulting from microvascular ischemia and resultant cell death.
Must Know — Most important microscopic feature
  • Thickened, hypertrophic cardiac muscles with widened transverse diameter accompanied by thickening, enlargement and squared nuclei.
  • Muscles are arranged in haphazard manner with multidirectional appearance (T or angulated shape).

Clinical Features p.18

  • Many individuals may be asymptomatic. Diagnosis may be incidental or identified during a screening examination.
  • Symptomatic patients: anginal pain, palpitation, dyspnea, syncope.
  • Harsh systolic ejection murmur — abnormal heart sounds and murmur may be elicited as a result of a left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.
Must Know — Mechanism of symptoms
  • Impaired diastolic filling of the hypertrophied LV → reduced chamber size, reduced stroke volume, decreased cardiac output.
  • Reduced stroke volume is due to impaired diastolic filling (consequence of a reduced chamber size) and reduced compliance of a massively hypertrophic LV.
Clinical complications
  • Atrial fibrillation with mural thrombus and embolization
  • Infective endocarditis (mitral valve)
  • Intractable cardiac failure
  • Ventricular arrhythmias producing sudden cardiac death

Restrictive Cardiomyopathy (RCMP)

Key Facts Must Know p.18

  • Rare, least common (5%).
  • Characterized by ventricular reduction in compliance → impaired ventricular filling during diastolic phase
    • Contractile systolic function of the LV is usually unaffected.
  • Systolic function, volume, and wall thickness of the left ventricle often remain normal.
  • Decreased LV ejection fraction, enlarged LA — atrial enlargement and increase in left atrial pressure occur due to impaired ventricular filling during diastole.
Must Know Characterized by diastolic dysfunction with restrictive ventricular wall movement resulting in abnormalities in the left ventricular diastolic relaxation.
Decreased cardiac compliance
→
Impaired ventricular filling during diastole (diastolic dysfunction)
→
Atrial enlargement and increase in left atrial pressure

Causes and Etiopathogenesis p.19

Primary / Idiopathic RCMPSecondary RCMP (Infiltrative CMP)
  • Endomyocardial fibrosis
  • Loeffler's endocarditis
  • Genetic and sporadic cases
    • Genetic (in 30%) with autosomal dominant mode, mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins including troponin and cardiac actin. Familial history reported in approximately 30% of cases.
  • Presents cardiac manifestations of a systemic disorder.
  • Amyloidosis (most common)
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Hemochromatosis
  • Scleroderma/progressive systemic sclerosis
  • Carcinoid heart disease
  • Glycogen storage disease
  • Radiation induced myopathy
  • Tumor metastasis
  • Anthracycline toxicity (drug-induced myopathy)
  • Immune reaction
  • Metabolic diseases
  • EMF and Loeffler's CMP are the most common global causes of RCMP affecting an estimated 12M people worldwide
    • More common in Africa.

Endomyocardial Fibrosis (EMF) Must Know p.19

  • Most common form of RCMP.
  • Principally a disease of children and young adults. Commonly found in Africa and other tropical areas.
  • Linked to nutritional deficiencies and inflammation related to parasitic infection worldwide.
  • Fibroelastic deposition in the endocardium, secondary mural thrombi
    • Ventricular thrombi may develop.
  • Characterized by fibrosis of the ventricular endocardium and subendocardium and involves the tricuspid and mitral valves.
Focal to diffuse cartilage-like fibroelastosis of the left and right endocardium
→
Wall stiffening
→
Loss of ventricular compliance during ventricular relaxation and diastole

Fibrous tissue markedly diminishes the volume and compliance of the affected chambers to cause restriction of wall movement during ventricular diastolic phase.

Loeffler's Eosinophilic Endomyocardial Disease (Loeffler's CMP) p.19

  • Severe prolonged eosinophilia due to any cause (e.g. allergy, autoimmune, or parasitic causes) → eosinophilic infiltration in the myocardium → toxicity of eosinophilic granule.
  • The intracytoplasmic granular content of activated eosinophils is responsible for the toxic damage to the heart.
StageFeatures
Initial StageAcute inflammatory phase characterized by fever and pancarditis
Intermediate StageFormation of LV and RV thrombus
Final StageAfter months to years, development of endocardial fibrosis
Release of toxic product of eosinophils
→
Endomyocardial necrosis
→
Scarring
→
Layering of endocardium by thrombus
→
Thrombotic fibrous organization

Secondary RCMP / Infiltrative CMP Must Know p.19

  • Abnormal deposits of substance (iron, amyloid, etc.) in the myocardium causing ventricular stiffening and diastolic dysfunction, conduction and coronary artery abnormalities
    • Secondarily affects the heart in a setting of systemic disease.
  • Leads to abnormality of contractility, conduction, and coronary blood flow.
  • Biventricular diastolic dysfunction causes intracardiac pressure to rise → progression to systolic dysfunction in advanced disease phase.
  • Diagnosed by endocardial biopsy, ECG or cardiac MRI. Treatment is largely supportive in many cases.
Must Know
  • Amyloidosis — most common secondary RCMP.
  • Myocardial wall becomes thickened and firm, rubbery and non-compliant → infiltration and accumulation of substance → restriction of the wall movement.

Morphology and Clinical Features of RCMP p.19

Gross (non-specific)

  • Bi-atrial dilatation — commonly observed due to restrictive ventricular filling and pressure overload
  • Stiff, firm, normal-sized ventricles (or slightly enlarged)
    • Normal sized or slightly enlarged heart
    • Non-dilated ventricular chamber. Myocardium may be largely unremarkable

Microscopic

  • Patchy or diffuse interstitial fibrosis
    • Identifiable depositions/infiltrations that may restrict the cardiac wall: Iron (hemochromatosis, hemosiderosis)
    • Amyloid
    • Eosinophils
    • Fibroelastic tissues
  • Cardiac imaging is increasingly used to characterize myocardial infiltrates
    • Myocardial biopsy can occasionally suggest a specific etiology.

Clinical features

  • S/S of left-sided and right-sided CHF with pulmonary and systemic congestion.
  • Thromboembolic phenomenon in 30% of cases.
  • Physical examination: bi-atrial enlargement, normal ventricular size (ventricles may be diffusely enlarged due to accumulated substance such as amyloid), significant diffuse LV hypertrophy.
  • Arrhythmia — complete heart blocks are common in RCMP.
  • Systemic manifestations in secondary RCMP (e.g. secondary amyloidosis in the liver, lungs, kidneys, and other organs).

Specific Forms of RCMP p.20-21

Fibroelastosis (Endomyocardial fibroelastosis)

  • Widespread thickening of the mural endocardium due to proliferation of collagen and elastic fibers.
  • Pathophysiology: deposition of a cellular fibrocartilaginous tissue in the subendothelial layer of the endocardium of both ventricles.
  • Gross: glistening, white appearance of the endocardium. Myocardial wall thickness appears normal
    • Valvular leaflets may be secondarily affected (thickening, adhesion, shortening of the papillary muscle → mitral valvular regurgitation)
    • Prone to mural thrombus.
  • Microscopic: thickening of the subendocardial layer by paucicellular fibroelastic tissue.

Hemosiderosis

  • Secondary RCMP. Deposit of iron in the parenchymatous tissues, related to systemic hemosiderosis.
  • Rust-brown discoloration due to (+) iron deposits
    • Stained with Prussian blue stain, giving a bluish and granular appearance microscopically.
  • Bi-atrial enlargement, non-dilated ventricular chambers, normal ventricular wall thickness.

Amyloidosis Must Know

  • Most common cause of RCMP in the US. Systemic or cardiac form of amyloidosis.
  • Produces RCMP due to the extracellular accumulation of amyloid protein fibrils that form insoluble β-pleated sheets.
    • Amyloid deposits (transthyretin) in interstitium: H/E stain: pink glassy
    • Congo red stain: apple green birefringence under polarized microscope.
  • Multisystem deposition of amyloid fibrils in the liver, kidney, bowels, nerve, skin, tongue, and heart
    • Cardiac involvement is common in the elderly.
  • Gross: ventricular walls typically thickened, sometimes with disproportionate septal thickening, and may mimic the appearance of HCMP. Atrial dilatation develops as a consequence of increased ventricular filling pressures and restrictive physiology.

Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Dysplasia/Cardiomyopathy (ARVC)

Key Facts Must Know p.21

This condition is a newly added classification according to WHO.

  • A disease of the heart muscle characterized by replacement of RV by fibro-fatty tissues, producing life-threatening arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.
  • Occurs in an estimated 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,250 people.
Must Know The fatty replacement interrupts normal electrical signals: electrical instability in the heart may cause irregular and potentially life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death.

Etiopathogenesis

  • A genetic factor is implicated: autosomal dominant inheritance involving genes encoding desmosomal junctional proteins at the intercalated disk (e.g., plakoglobin), known as desmosomal genes.
    • Desmosomes attach heart muscle cells to one another, providing strength to the myocardium and playing a role in signaling between neighboring myocardial cells.
    • Without normal desmosomes, cells of the myocardium detach from one another and die.
  • These changes primarily affect the myocardium surrounding the RV. The damaged myocardium is replaced by fat and scar tissue.
  • As the fibro-fatty tissue builds up, the walls of the RV become stretched out, preventing the heart from pumping effectively, and the electrical signals are disrupted → life-threatening arrhythmia.

Symptoms of ARVC p.21

  • Generally asymptomatic in early stages. Symptoms usually appear in adulthood: chest palpitations, light-headedness, fainting (syncope), chest pain.
  • Over time: shortness of breath and abnormal swelling in the legs and abdomen
    • Severe damage in later stages → RV failure.
  • Aneurysmal dilatation is present in 50% of cases — occurs in the diaphragm, apical area, and infundibulum, known as the triangle of dysplasia.
  • With progression, RV failure can occur, and eventually the LV fails → biventricular failure. Further progresses to CHF, atrial fibrillation, and thromboembolic events.

Morphology of ARVC Must Know p.21-22

Gross

  • Most important pathologic change: involvement of the RV with replacement of the RV wall by a thick coat of fibro-fatty tissue.
    • External appearance: lardaceous appearance of the RV. LV does not have a similar coating.
  • Heart weight, LV, and ventricular septum are usually normal. RV enlargement is a constant feature.
  • RV appears yellow to white due to fatty or fibro-fatty infiltration
    • Fatty changes can be focal (20%) or diffuse (80%). (+) thinning of myocardial wall.
Must Know — Pathognomonic feature Aneurysms of the RV free wall, whether single or multiple, are considered a pathognomonic feature.

Microscopic

Must Know
  • Characteristic fatty infiltration of the RV wall with minimal mononuclear inflammation.
  • Take note of the remaining small snippets of the myocardial fibers on the RV, which is largely replaced by fatty tissue.
  • Fibro-fatty or fat replacement of the myocardial muscle
    • The muscles may show a moth-eaten appearance, mild inflammation, and scarring.

B. Myocarditis

Definition Must Know p.22

  • Defined by WHO/IFSC as an inflammatory disease of the heart muscle, diagnosed by established histological, immunological, and immunohistochemical criteria.
  • A diverse group of pathologic entities in which infectious microorganisms and/or a primary inflammatory process cause myocardial injury. Must be distinguished from other cardiac conditions (e.g., ischemic heart disease) wherein myocardial inflammation is secondary to other causes.
  • An inflammatory response within the myocardium that is NOT secondary to an ischemic event or cardiac rejection in the setting of transplantation.
  • The presence of myocyte necrosis is required for certain types, specifically lymphocytic myocarditis. Damage is mediated both by direct invasion of the myocardium and by immune insult.
  • Epidemiology: present in 8.6-12% of autopsied cases of sudden death in young adults
    • Incidence of biopsy-proven myocarditis in unexplained heart failure: 9.6%.
Must Know — Most important finding Presence of inflammation that is related to a biologic agent or a disease process and not in relation to localized effects related to primary myocardial injury.

Causes of Myocarditis p.22

Myocarditis usually falls into the following categories: infectious, immune-mediated, and unknown or idiopathic.

InfectionsImmune-Mediated ReactionsUnknown
  • Viruses (e.g., coxsackievirus, echovirus, influenza, HIV, cytomegalovirus)
  • Chlamydiae (e.g., Chlamydophila psittaci)
  • Rickettsiae (e.g., Rickettsia typhi, typhus fever)
  • Bacteria (e.g., Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Neisseria meningococcus, Borrelia [Lyme disease])
  • Fungi (e.g., Candida)
  • Protozoa (e.g., Trypanosoma cruzi [Chagas disease], toxoplasmosis)
  • Helminths (e.g., trichinosis)
  • Postviral
  • Poststreptococcal (rheumatic fever)
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Drug hypersensitivity (e.g., methyldopa, sulfonamides)
  • Transplant rejection
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapies
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Giant cell myocarditis
  • In >50% of patients, myocarditis is believed to be post-viral immune-related, even in the absence of demonstrable viral antigens
    • In viral myocarditis, an identifiable infectious organism is present 10-100% of the time.
  • Drug-associated myocarditis is classified under immune-mediated
    • Implicated drugs: clozapine, penicillin, ampicillin, hydrochlorothiazide, methyldopa, sulfonamide drugs.
  • Radiation therapy and insect bites are reported to cause heart injury as well
    • Systemic diseases: SLE, mixed connective tissue disease, rheumatoid arthritis.
Must Know Two important idiopathic forms: sarcoidosis and giant cell myocarditis.

Infectious Etiologic Agents Must Know p.23

1. Viruses

  • Most prevalent etiologic biologic agents that can affect and infect the heart.
  • Coxsackie viruses A and B, other enteroviruses: account for most cases.
  • Cytomegalovirus, HIV, influenza, COVID: less common.
  • Identification through serologic studies or viral nucleic acid sequences (PCR) in myocardial biopsies.
  • Viruses cause myocardial injury either by direct cytopathic effect or by eliciting a destructive immune response. Inflammatory cytokines can cause myocardial dysfunction out of proportion to the degree of actual myocyte damage.
  • Most viral myocarditis are self-limiting, but sometimes elicit a protracted post-inflammatory immune-mediated myocarditis.

2. Parasites

  • Trypanosoma cruzi, the agent of Chagas disease: endemic in some regions of South America with myocardial involvement in most infected individuals. 10% of patients die during an acute attack
    • Others develop a chronic immune-mediated myocarditis that may progress to chronic cardiac disease in 10-20 years.
  • Trichinosis (Trichinella spiralis) is the most common helminthic disease associated with myocarditis. The parasite can infect and encyst the heart muscles, eliciting an eosinophilic type of myocarditis.
  • Toxoplasmosis can also affect the heart.

3. Bacteria

  • Lyme disease: vector tick-borne disease caused by spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. Initially fever, skin rash, joint pains, neurological symptoms
    • Myocardial involvement in 5% of cases, usually presenting with palpitations, chest pains, arrhythmia, particularly AV block. Assessed through tick exposure and Borrelia serologic markers.
  • Diphtheric myocarditis: myocardial injury is a consequence of toxin-mediated release by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Occurs as a complication in about 10-25% of cases and is responsible for 50-60% of deaths from this disease
    • Pathologic changes include fatty, hyaline changes, sometimes with toxic myolysis of cardiac myocytes, and inflammation.
  • Pathogenesis pathways:
    • direct damage to myocardium
    • toxin-mediated cardiac injury
    • immune-mediated
    • idiopathic.

Morphology of Myocarditis Must Know p.23-24

Gross

  • Heart may appear grossly normal, with normal dimensions and non-dilated chambers
    • Inflammation may be focal or patchy, not apparent on gross examination.
  • Depending on the etiologic agent, there may be concomitant pleural effusion and pericardial inflammation, as seen in bacterial or viral myocarditis.
  • Associated mural thrombus may be appreciated, reflecting the risk for thrombosis with damaged endocardium.
  • Late stages may show focal or diffuse fibrosis.
Must Know — Gross appearance
  • Severe myocarditis: softening and flabbiness of the heart with pallor and focal hemorrhagic areas, imparting a mottled appearance.
  • Most instances: the heart may be enlarged, soft and flabby, with dilated ventricular chambers, and reddish, beefy discoloration.

Microscopic

  • The inflammatory pattern is interstitial in location
    • The location of the infiltrates can provide information on the nature of the etiologic agent
    • Some overlap exists, no finding is specific for a single etiology.
  • Histologic patterns:
    • Lymphocytic (including viral and autoimmune forms)
    • Eosinophilic (parasitic and hypersensitivity type)
    • Granulomatous (cardiac sarcoidosis and giant-cell myocarditis)
    • Neutrophilic (bacterial, fungal, and early forms of viral myocarditis)
  • Other associated findings: edema, vascular congestion. The presence of viral inclusions or parasites help identify the offending organism.
Must Know — Hallmark of myocarditis Presence of focal myocyte necrosis surrounded by inflammatory cells.
Must Know — Dallas criteria (biopsy-based diagnosis, 1987)
  • Presence of interstitial inflammation permeating in the myocardial wall
  • Presence of focal myocytic necrosis or degeneration
Inflammatory cellIndicates
Polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs)Bacterial infections
LymphocytesAutoimmune and viral infections
EosinophilsHypersensitivity or parasitic infections

Clinical Features p.24

  • The clinical spectrum is broad: asymptomatic (complete recovery without sequelae) to symptomatic (precipitous onset of heart failure and arrhythmias, occasionally followed by sudden death)
    • In between: fatigue, dyspnea, palpitations, chest pain, precordial discomfort, fever.
  • Complications: CHF, arrhythmias, pericarditis, late complications of cardiomyopathies, sudden cardiac death.
  • Most cases are acute and self-limited: patients heal and recover spontaneously
    • Patients typically show ECG alterations, cardiac enzyme elevations, and evidence of a systemic inflammatory process (arthralgia, malaise, pharyngitis, tonsillitis, URTI).
  • In most instances, there is no indication for endomyocardial biopsy and the diagnosis is assigned clinically.
  • Acute fulminant myocarditis: rapidly deteriorating course, acute presentation with rapid onset of heart failure that may cause sudden death
    • Myocardial involvement is often diffuse.
Must Know
  • Infection is the most common cause of myocarditis with viral infections being far more common than bacterial infections.
  • Associated pericarditis is common in bacterial and viral forms.

Laboratory Diagnosis p.25

ECG
ECG
Used to document the presence of arrhythmias
Inflammation biomarkers
Inflammation biomarkers
ESR, CRP
Cardiac injury biomarkers
Cardiac injury biomarkers
Trop I, CK, BNP
Serologic markers
Serologic markers
Ag-Ab titers
Molecular diagnostics
Molecular diagnostics
PCR
Imaging
Imaging
MRI, ECG — establish the functional, radiologic, and morphologic state of the lesion
Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB)
Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB)
Gold standard for diagnosis. 4-5 biopsy samples from more than one area of the RV septum and myocardium are needed because myocarditis can be a focal disease process. Analyzed using light microscopy and ancillary immunohistochemical assays.

Other Types of Myocarditis

Giant Cell Myocarditis (GCM) Must Know p.25

  • Idiopathic in nature
    • Also known as Fiedler's myocarditis.
  • Heterogeneous inflammatory infiltrate composed of abundant lymphocytes, some eosinophils and plasma cells, occasional neutrophils, and scattered prominent giant cells.
  • Has an aggressive clinical course. Patients may die of CHF. Cardiac transplantation may be necessary.
Must Know — Distinctive characteristics
  • Presence of multinucleated giant cells is a sine qua non requirement for the diagnosis of GCM.
  • Another important feature: extensive myocardial necrosis with fragmentation of the cardiac muscles.

Hypersensitivity / Eosinophilic Myocarditis Must Know p.25

  • Numerous eosinophils in the interstitial inflammatory infiltrate, accompanied by macrophages.
  • No or little necrosis of the cardiac myocytes.
  • No granulomas or multinucleated giant cells can be identified.
  • Clinical symptoms are fewer and are usually associated with adverse drug reactions towards methyldopa.

Acute Viral Myocarditis p.25

  • Characterized by edema
  • (+) Mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates
  • (+) Myocyte degeneration and necrosis
  • Viral inclusions may be present
Must Know — Summary: Myocarditis (lecture summary marked ❗)
  • An inflammatory disease of the myocardium that results in acute myocyte injury.
  • Viruses are the most common cause of myocarditis.
  • Gross: heart is normal or dilated, diffuse or patchy lesions, ventricular myocardium flabby and mottled due to pale foci or minute hemorrhagic lesions, appears beefy-red due to inflammation, mural thrombi.
  • Microscopy: interstitial inflammatory infiltrate, edema, focal necrosis.
  • 3 types:
    • Giant Cell Myocarditis — multinucleated giant cells and inflammatory cells. Aggressive clinical course: indication of cardiac transplant.
    • Hypersensitivity Myocarditis — interstitial infiltrate: macrophages, eosinophils
      • No or little necrosis, no granulomas
      • Associated with ADR: classically methyldopa.
    • Acute Viral Myocarditis — edema, mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates, myocyte degeneration and necrosis.

C. COVID-19 Heart Disease

Overview p.25

  • The heart is one of the target organ complications of COVID-19
    • Increasing reports of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality related to COVID-19 infection.
  • Complications of acute cardiac injury were recognized in 12-18% of COVID-19 patients
    • Incidence was approximately 13x higher in ICU/severe patients than in non-ICU/severe patients.
  • The presence of CVS complications of COVID is associated with poor prognosis and increased mortality.
  • Risk factors: DM, obesity, HTN, CVD (e.g. IHD, CHF, valvular heart failure), increasing age.

Coronavirus and Viral Structure Must Know p.25-26

  • Causative agent of COVID-19: SARS-CoV-2, family of Coronaviruses, Betacoronavirus.
  • Enveloped RNA viruses distributed broadly among humans, other mammals, and birds
    • Can cause respiratory, enteric, hepatic, and neurologic diseases
    • Etiologic agents for SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV epidemics.
  • Has an envelope that bears crown-like spikes (20 nm in length) that resemble the corona of the sun under an electron microscope.
  • Within the envelope is a (+)ssRNA molecule bound to a nucleocapsid (N) protein. The nucleoprotein wraps the RNA genome to form a coiled tubular structure.
Structural ProteinFunction of Protein
Nucleocapsid Protein (N)Bound to RNA genome to make up nucleocapsid
Spike Protein (S)Critical for binding of host cell receptors to facilitate entry of host cell. Target of the neutralizing antibody.
Envelope Protein (E)Interacts with M to form a viral envelope
Membrane Protein (M)The central organizer of CoV assembly. Determines the shape of the viral envelope.
Must Know The spike structural protein (S) is anchored in the envelope and is critical for the binding of host receptors to facilitate the entry of the virus to the host cell.

Progression of COVID-19 Infection Must Know p.26-27

From the extracellular environment, the virus attaches to the host cell by way of the spike protein S, using the ACE2 receptor (angiotensin converting enzyme 2).

Phase I: Early Infection StagePhase II: Pulmonary StagePhase III: Hyperinflammation Stage
  • Virus enters the host cells (respiratory epithelial cells and/or alveolar type 2 cells) → proliferates intracellularly → body produces innate immunity.
  • S/S: fever, rhinorrhea, cough, fatigue, constitutional flu-like symptoms.
  • With a good immune system, adaptive immunity can overcome the virus → resolution of symptoms.
  • Virus infects the alveolar cells → pulmonary cell injury.
  • Usually occurs among people with comorbidities: DM, HTN, CVD, obesity, poor immune status.
  • Pulmonary vessel dilatation, increased endothelial permeability, leukocyte recruitment → further pulmonary damage (COVID pneumonia) → hypoxemia and increased cardiovascular stress.
  • Cytokine storm: aggressive inflammatory response due to release of a large amount of proinflammatory cytokines.
  • Hyperactive host response → multi-organ damage, ARDS (hyaline membranes within alveolar walls), multi-organ failure (kidney, liver, brain, heart).
  • Heart often affected: increased cardiovascular stress and load → acute cardiac injury (myocarditis, ischemia, infarct) and heart failure.
  • Increased risk of DIC — culminating event in cytokine storm.
Laboratory parameters used to determine the presence of cytokine storm CRP, procalcitonin, D-dimer, ferritin, cardiac markers (troponin and BNP)

Risk factors for cardiovascular complications

  • Diabetes mellitus, Obesity, Hypertension, Underlying CVD, Age.
  • Patients with underlying CVD are more likely to have cardiac injury (troponin elevation) compared with patients without CVD (54.5% vs 13.2%). Mortality was 7.6% without underlying CVD and normal Tn, compared to 69.4% with pre-existing CVD and elevated troponin.
    • Patients with pre-existing CVD may not be more susceptible to contracting SARS-CoV-2, but they are prone to more severe complications with increased mortality.
  • Age: both a risk factor for CVD and a determinant of COVID-19 fatality (14.8% in patients older than 80 years).

Pathophysiology of COVID Heart Disease Must Know p.27

  • SARS-CoV-2 uses the ACE2 protein for ligand binding before entering the cell via receptor-mediated endocytosis.
  • ACE2 is a membrane protein with many physiological functions in the lungs, heart, kidneys, and other organs
    • Highly expressed in type 2 lung alveolar cells (respiratory symptoms).
  • More than 7.5% of myocardial cells have positive ACE2 expression (single cell RNA sequencing), which could mediate SARS-CoV-2 entry into cardiomyocytes and cause direct cardiotoxicity.

Plausible mechanisms of cardiovascular injury (likely multifactorial)

  1. Direct cardiotoxicity — SARS-CoV-2 viral particles identified by RT-PCR in cardiac tissues.
  2. Virally driven hyperinflammation with cytokine release → vascular inflammation, plaque instability, myocardial inflammation, hypercoagulable state, thrombosis → fulminant myocarditis and activated cytokine storm syndrome.
  3. Direct myocardial suppression.
  4. Other systemic consequences of COVID-19: sepsis and DIC.
Must Know An extremely robust cytokine storm is the core pathophysiological mechanism of fulminant myocarditis affected by COVID-19.
Direct damage to the myocardiumIndirect damage through cytokine storm
  • Produces myocarditis, heart failure, and arrhythmia.
  • Mediated through downregulation of ACE2, vascular endothelial cell dysfunction, microvascular dysfunction (pericyte injury), and hypoxemia.
  • As a consequence of myocarditis, thromboembolism and metabolic disorder.
  • Mediated through the release of cytokines (IL-6, etc.), coagulopathy, and insulin resistance.

Cardiovascular manifestations and figures from the lecture

  • Although the main presentation of COVID-19 is viral pneumonia, it can induce myocardial injury, myocarditis, arrhythmias, acute coronary syndrome, and thromboembolism. Cardiovascular comorbidities (HTN, coronary artery disease) are associated with high mortality.
  • Heart failure: documented in 23% of patients who died in Wuhan, China
    • Due to severe myocarditis or pre-existing CVD with systolic dysfunction and cardiac decompensation.
  • Arrhythmias: found in 17% of patients
    • Associated with fulminant myocarditis with atrial and ventricular tachyarrhythmias and heart block.
  • Venous thromboembolism and DIC: occurred in 71% of patients who died of severe COVID-19.
  • Cytokine release syndrome (CRS): severe COVID-19 shows elevated inflammatory cytokines
    • Postmortem: tissue necrosis, interstitial infiltrations with macrophages and monocytes in the lung, heart, and GI mucosa.
  • Metabolic syndromes (obesity, diabetes): higher risk of CVD in COVID-19.
Figure 62 — Bidirectional interaction between cardiovascular disease and COVID-19 (should know)

Clinical Manifestations p.28

  • Elevation of cardiac biomarkers: troponin, BNP
  • Elevated inflammatory biomarkers: CRP, ferritin, D-dimer, procalcitonin
  • Ischemic myocardial injury: AMI, angina pectoris
  • Cardiac arrhythmia
  • Arterial and venous thromboembolism
  • In fulminant cardiovascular COVID-19: cardiogenic shock and arrest

Pathologic Changes of COVID Heart Disease p.28

  1. Direct damage to myocardial cells, inducing focal myocardial necrosis and mononuclear interstitial inflammation.
