  2. Ischemic myocardial injury — the hypercoagulable state in cytokine storm syndrome may increase the risk of plaque rupture and thrombus formation → ischemic type of myocardial necrosis and infarction.
  3. Myocardial injury with DIC — life-threatening, present in 71% of patients who died of COVID-19
    • A marker of severe sepsis
    • DIC perpetuates multi-organ damage through thrombosis, reduced perfusion, and bleeding
    • Implicated in thrombosis of coronary arteries, focal necrosis of the myocardium, and severe cardiac dysfunction.
  4. Non-ischemic myocardial injury and stress-induced CMP.
  • Microscopic findings:
    • intramyocardial thrombi (19% of patients)
    • myocardial ischemia with myocardial necrosis
    • myocarditis.

VI. Valvular Heart Disease

Causes and Types p.28

Causes of valvular heart disease
    • Congenital valvular heart disease: congenital bicuspid valve
    • congenital calcific aortic stenosis
    • mitral valve prolapse
    • Acquired valvular heart disease: rheumatic valvulitis
    • infective endocarditis
TypeDefinition
StenosisFailure of the valve to open completely, impeding forward blood flow
Insufficiency / RegurgitationFailure of the valve to close completely, resulting in reversal of flow
Mixed stenosis/regurgitationBoth present
Singular vs combined
  • Singular valve disease
  • Combined, multiple valvular diseases
Functional regurgitationValvular incompetence due to ventricular dilatation
Table 4 — Etiology of Acquired Heart Valve Disease (should know)
Mitral Valve DiseaseAortic Valve Disease
  • Mitral Stenosis
  • Post inflammatory scarring (rheumatic heart disease)
  • Aortic Stenosis
  • Post inflammatory scarring (rheumatic heart disease)
  • Senile calcific aortic stenosis
  • Calcification of congenitally deformed valve
  • Mitral Regurgitation
  • Abnormalities of leaflets and commissures: post inflammatory scarring, infective endocarditis, mitral valve prolapse, "Fen-Phen"-induced valvular fibrosis
  • Abnormalities of tensor apparatus: rupture of papillary muscle, papillary muscle dysfunction (fibrosis), rupture of chordae tendineae
  • Abnormalities of LV cavity and/or annulus: LV enlargement (myocarditis, dilated cardiomyopathy), calcification of mitral ring
  • Aortic Regurgitation
  • Intrinsic valvular disease: post inflammatory scarring (rheumatic heart disease), infective endocarditis
  • Aortic disease: degenerative aortic dilation, syphilitic aortitis, ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, Marfan syndrome

A. Degenerative Valvular Calcification

Calcific Aortic Valve Stenosis Must Know p.29

Must Know Most frequent valve abnormality.
Congenital
Congenital
Bicuspid or unicuspid
Acquired
Acquired
Atherosclerotic calcification, RHD, age-related degeneration
Morphology
Morphology
Heaped calcified masses within aortic cusps, no commissural fusion
Clinical presentation
Clinical presentation
Increased LV pressure leading to concentric LVH, angina, syncope, CHF

Congenital Bicuspid Aortic Valve Calcification p.29

  • Unequal sized bicuspid valve with midline "raphe"
    • Predisposed to: degenerative calcification → stenosis
    • infective endocarditis → incompetence
  • Associated with: aortic coarctation, aneurysm, dissection

Mitral Annular Calcification p.29

  • Calcified nodular deposits in the annular ring
  • Common in elderly women with myxomatous MV
  • Clinical effects: regurgitation, stenosis, arrhythmias, embolism, sudden death due to calcium deposits in the conducting system
Must Know — Gross morphology Irregular, stony, hard nodules behind the MV leaflets.

B. Infective Endocarditis (IE)

Definition and Causes Must Know p.29

  • Colonization of heart valves and mural endocardium by microbiological agents, forming bulky vegetations.
  • Vegetations contain: thrombotic material, inflammatory cells, microbiologic organisms.
    • Causes: Bacteria (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus, Pneumococci, etc.)
    • Fungi (Aspergillosis, Candida, Mucormycosis, etc.)
    • Rickettsia
    • Chlamydia.
Acute Infective EndocarditisSubacute Infective Endocarditis
  • Caused by highly virulent organisms
  • Arises in a normal valve
  • Produces necrotizing, ulcerative, and destructive lesions
  • Bulky, friable vegetations
  • More severe clinical signs and symptoms (higher morbidity)
  • Occurs in previously diseased valves (congenital valve anomaly, RHD, MV prolapse, etc.)
  • Caused by low virulent organisms (Enterococci, Streptococcus viridans)
  • Insidious clinical onset

Morphology, Clinical Features, Complications p.30

Morphology

  • Friable vegetations on valves
    • Necrotizing, ulcerating lesions, or ring abscesses.
  • Frequently involves the AV and MV. TV among drug mainliners.
  • Vegetations contain bacterial colonies, fibrin, platelets, RBCs, and WBCs.

Clinical features

  • Fever, weight loss, fatigue, anorexia, changing murmurs
  • Laboratory diagnosis: leukocytosis, positive blood culture

Complications

Cardiac
Cardiac
CHF, valve insufficiency/stenosis, myocardial ring abscess, suppurative pericarditis, valvular rupture
Embolic
Embolic
Roth spots, subungual and cerebrovascular hemorrhages
Renal
Renal
Embolic infarcts, focal/diffuse glomerulonephritis, abscesses

C. Nonbacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis (NBTE)

Key Facts Must Know p.30

  • AKA Marantic endocarditis.
  • Sterile vegetations. Associated with debilitated patients, carcinoma, and sepsis.
  • Pathogenesis:
    • hypercoagulable states
    • malignancy
    • instrumentation
  • Morphology:
    • sterile thrombi deposits
    • single or multiple vegetations
    • along lines of closure
  • Histology:
    • bland thrombi attached to the underlying valve
    • non-invasive vegetations (no inflammation)
Must Know Characterized by deposition of fibrin, platelets, and other cellular elements of blood (thrombus) on the valve leaflets.

D. Libman-Sacks Endocarditis (LSE) p.30

  • Associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
  • Affects MV and TV.
  • Sterile, small vegetations located on the undersurface of cords or mural endocardium of atria or ventricles.
  • Histology: finely granular, fibrinous eosinophilic material containing hematoxylin bodies (degraded nuclear material)
    • Fibrinous necrosis of valve.

E. Carcinoid Heart Disease p.30

  • Cardiac manifestation of carcinoid syndrome: episodic skin flushing, cramps, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
  • Elaboration of serotonin, histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandin.
    • CVS lesions: involves PV and TV
    • endocardial thickening/fibrosis.

The Four Major Forms of Vegetative Endocarditis p.32

F. Rheumatic Fever and Rheumatic Heart Disease

Definition and Jones Criteria Must Know p.31

Acute, immunologically mediated, multi-system inflammatory disease following group A (beta-hemolytic) streptococcal pharyngitis.

Major criteria (Jones)Minor criteria (Jones)
  • Migratory polyarthritis
  • Carditis
  • Subcutaneous nodules
  • Erythema marginatum
  • Sydenham's chorea
  • Fever
  • Arthralgia
  • History of sore throat, increased ASO
  • Increased acute phase reactants: ESR, CRP
Must Know — Diagnosis
  • Combination of 2 major criteria of Jones
  • Combination of one major and two minor criteria of Jones
Exam Trap (from lecture concept checkpoint) Rheumatic fever is caused by group A streptococci, not group B.

Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) Must Know p.31

Pathogenesis

  • A hypersensitivity reaction induced by group A streptococci.
  • Antibodies directed against the M proteins of certain strains of streptococci cross-react with glycoprotein antigens in the heart, joints, and other tissues.
Must Know — Morphology Aschoff bodies, pancarditis, myocarditis, fibrinous pericarditis, endocarditis, verrucal vegetations on lines of closure, called MacCallum plaques.

Chronic Rheumatic Fever (CRF) Must Know p.31

Morphology

  • Multivalvular (MV, AV, TV)
  • Commissural fusion of cusps leading to stenosis
  • Shortening/thickening of chordae tendineae
  • Fibrosis and subendocardial fibrosis
Must Know "Fish mouth deformity" — chronic rheumatic fever is distinguishable by a fish mouth deformity of the valves.

G. Mitral Valve Prolapse (MVP)

Key Facts Must Know p.32

  • AKA myxomatous degeneration of the MV. "Floppy valve syndrome".
  • MV is enlarged, redundant, hooded, or floppy. Tendency to prolapse into the LA during systole.
  • Pathogenesis: idiopathic, theorized to be a developmental anomaly of connective tissue
    • Associated diseases: Marfan's syndrome, scoliosis, high arch palate.
Must Know Most common form of valvular disease in industrialized countries.

Morphology

Must Know — Characteristic anatomic change Hooding/ballooning of the mitral leaflets.
  • MV thickening, fibrosis, calcification
    • Annular dilatation is common.
  • May involve TV in 20-30% of cases.
  • Microscopic features: myxomatous degeneration of MV.
  • Secondary changes: fibrosis of MV leaflet, LV subendocardial fibrosis, jet lesions of LA, thrombi on leaflets/LA.

Clinical features

  • Majority are asymptomatic.
  • Mid-systolic click (snapping and tensing of everted cusps)
    • Late systolic or holosystolic murmur.
  • Symptoms: chest pain, dyspnea, fatigue, depression.
  • Complications: infective endocarditis, mitral insufficiency, thrombo-embolic complications, arrhythmias.
Clinical Cue (from lecture quiz)
  • If you see a clinical finding of a midsystolic click, you should know it is a mitral valve prolapse
    • Midsystolic click = mitral valve prolapse.
  • The cause of the ballooning effect of the mitral valve is an underlying myxomatous degeneration of valve leaflets.

VII. Pericarditis

TypeCausesFeaturesSequelae / notes
A. Serous
  • RHD
  • SLE
  • uremia
  • and viral
Scanty inflammation. (+/-) pericardial serous effusionOrganization into fibrous adhesions are rare sequelae
B. FibrinousUremia, RHD, post-radiation, post-infarction (Dressler syndrome)The most common type of pericarditis. Shaggy and rough pericardium. "Bread and butter" pericarditisSequelae: resolution, lysis, or organization
C. HemorrhagicMost commonly caused by the spread of a malignant neoplasm to the pericardial space. Other causes: TB, bacterial agents, bleeding diathesis, tumorsExudate composed of blood mixed with fibrinous and suppurative effusion
  • Cytologic examination of fluid from a pericardial tap often reveals neoplastic cells. Often follows cardiac surgery and may cause significant blood loss or tamponade requiring reoperation
  • Clinical significance similar to fibrinous or suppurative
D. Purulent / Suppurative
  • Reflects an active infection caused by microbial invasion of the pericardial space.
  • Pathways of spread:
    • direct extension from neighboring infections (lungs, mediastinum, aorta)
    • hematogenous seeding
    • lymphatic extension
    • iatrogenic (seeding during cardiotomy)
  • Exudate ranges from thin cloudy fluid to frank pus (up to 500 mL)
  • Tuberculous pericarditis can exhibit foci of caseation. Microscopically: acute inflammatory reaction, sometimes extends to surrounding structures (mediastinopericarditis)
  • Complete resolution is infrequent
  • Organization by scarring is the usual outcome
  • Intense inflammation and scarring frequently produce constrictive pericarditis. Marked systemic symptoms: spiking fevers and rigors
E. Healed—Adhesive mediastinopericarditis: obliteration of pericardial sac with adhesion to the parietal pericardiumConstrictive pericarditis: obliterated sac with encasement by dense fibrous tissue
Must Know — Pericarditis anchors
  • Serous pericarditis: caused by RHD, SLE, uremia, and viral.
  • Fibrinous pericarditis: the most common type of pericarditis. "Bread and butter" pericarditis.
  • Hemorrhagic pericarditis: most commonly caused by the spread of a malignant neoplasm to the pericardial space.
Exam Trap (lecture quiz)
  • A pericardium with caseous material points to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (caseous pericarditis), not rheumatic fever, Staphylococcus aureus, or Coxsackie virus.
  • Pericarditis types listed in the quiz rationale: serous
  • fibrinous, serofibrinous
  • purulent/suppurative
  • hemorrhagic
  • caseous.

VIII. Cardiac Neoplasm

Overview p.33

  • Rare. Most are benign.
  • Malignant tumors: 5% — angiosarcomas, rhabdomyosarcomas.
  • Benign tumors: 80-90% of primary tumors of the heart
    • Descending order of frequency: myxomas, fibromas, lipomas, papillary fibroelastomas, rhabdomyomas.

A. Myxoma Must Know p.33-34

Must Know
  • Most common primary cardiac tumor in adults.
  • Usual location: fossa ovalis in the atrial septum.
  • Peculiar vessel-like or gland-like structures are characteristic.
  • Benign neoplasm arising from primitive multipotent mesenchymal cells.
  • Familial syndromes: activating mutations in the GNAS1 gene (Gsα, with McCune-Albright syndrome) or null mutations in PRKAR1A (Carney complex).
  • About 90% are located in the left atrium, with a left-to-right ratio of approximately 4:1.
  • Complications: ball-valve obstruction, embolization.
  • Gross:
    • usually single
    • size small to large (up to 10 cm)
    • sessile or pedunculated, globular, hard to soft, and myxoid.
  • Histology: stellate or globular myxoma cells embedded within an abundant acid mucopolysaccharide ground substance. Hemorrhage and mononuclear inflammation are usually present.
Exam Trap (lecture quiz) Myxoma is NOT aggressive or clinically malignant. The correct associations are: 90% in the left atrium, embolization is a usual complication, most common primary cardiac tumor in adults.

B. Rhabdomyoma Must Know p.34

Must Know
  • Most frequent primary cardiac tumor in children.
  • Routine histologic processing removes glycogen, producing "Spider" cells.
  • Most arise from the ventricular chamber. Can cause valvular or outflow tract obstruction.
  • Gross:
    • gray-white, fleshy, myocardial masses
    • usually located in the LV and RV or the right side of the heart
    • protrudes into ventricular chambers.
  • Histology: composed of bizarre, markedly enlarged myocytes with large collections of glycogen.
    • Spider cells: large, rounded, or polygonal cells with cytoplasmic glycogen vacuoles separated by strands of cytoplasm running from the plasma membrane to the centrally located nucleus.
Lecture-Specific Note — Hypertensive heart disease (mentioned in the quiz rationale)
  • Systemic HHD: it is the LV that is thickened (concentric LVH).
  • Pulmonary HHD (Cor Pulmonale): the RV is primarily affected
    • Acute cor pulmonale — RV dilation after massive pulmonary embolization
    • Chronic cor pulmonale — long standing pulmonary RV hypertrophy rather than dilation (chronic RV pressure overload, COPD, pulmonary artery disease, chest wall motion impairment).
  • Normal thickness: LV 1.5 cm, RV 0.5 cm. When LV and RV look almost equal in thickness, there is RV hypertrophy.

Fastest final recall of the must-know content. Red-exclamation points from the lecture are kept in the lecture's wording.

Core Definitions

  • Congenital heart disease: structural anomalies of heart and great vessels present at birth due to faulty embryogenesis
    • Occurs at the 1st trimester, 3rd to 8th week of AOG.
  • Shunt: abnormal communication between chambers (VSD, ASD) or between blood vessels (PDA).
  • Cardiomyopathy: heart disease resulting from a primary abnormality in the myocardium
    • Diagnosis of exclusion (exclude ischemic, myocarditis, hypertensive, valvular).
  • Myocarditis: inflammatory disease of the heart muscle (WHO/IFSC)
    • Inflammation NOT secondary to ischemia or transplant rejection
    • Most important finding: inflammation related to a biologic agent or disease process.
  • Infective endocarditis: colonization of heart valves and mural endocardium by microbiological agents, forming bulky vegetations.
  • NBTE: deposition of fibrin, platelets, and other cellular elements of blood (thrombus) on the valve leaflets
    • Sterile.
  • Rheumatic fever: acute, immunologically mediated, multi-system inflammatory disease following group A (beta-hemolytic) streptococcal pharyngitis.
  • Stenosis = failure to open completely
    • Regurgitation = failure to close completely
    • Functional regurgitation = incompetence due to ventricular dilatation.

Must Know — Fetal pressure switch (ASD)
  • Fetal life: lungs nonfunctional, pulmonary pressure greater than systemic → RA pressure greater than LA → valve of foramen ovale normally open.
  • At birth: lung expansion → pulmonary vascular pressures drop → RA pressure falls below LA → valve of foramen ovale closes, usually permanently sealed before adulthood
    • When this persists → ASD.
  • PFO closes in 75% at birth, 80% by 2 years, persists into adulthood in ~25%.

Mechanisms (short flows)

  • L-R shunt: left (high pressure) → right (low pressure) → right volume overload → RA dilatation + RVH → pulmonary HTN → shunt reversal → cyanosis (Eisenmenger).
  • TOF: pulmonary stenosis → RV outflow obstruction → RV → LV via VSD, bypassing lungs → early cyanosis
    • RVH overcomes the gradient.
  • HCMP symptoms: impaired diastolic filling of hypertrophied LV → reduced chamber size → reduced stroke volume → decreased CO.
  • RCMP: ↓ compliance → impaired diastolic filling → atrial enlargement, ↑ LA pressure.
  • EMF: cartilage-like fibroelastosis → wall stiffening → loss of ventricular compliance.
  • Loeffler's: eosinophil toxic granules → endomyocardial necrosis → scarring → thrombus layering → thrombotic fibrous organization
    • Stages: fever/pancarditis → LV/RV thrombus → endocardial fibrosis.
  • ARVC: desmosomal defect → myocytes detach and die → fat and scar replace RV → stretched RV + disrupted electrical signals → ventricular arrhythmia / SCD.
  • ARF: group A strep → antibodies vs M protein cross-react with glycoprotein antigens in heart, joints, other tissues.
  • COVID heart: spike S → ACE2 → receptor-mediated endocytosis → direct cardiotoxicity, hyperinflammation/cytokine storm, direct myocardial suppression, sepsis/DIC. Cytokine storm = core mechanism of fulminant myocarditis.

Myocarditis — Must Know Block

Must Know
  • Viruses most prevalent agents
    • Coxsackie A and B, other enteroviruses account for most cases
    • Infection most common cause, viral far more common than bacterial.
  • Two important idiopathic forms: sarcoidosis and giant cell myocarditis.
  • Trichinosis = most common helminthic disease with myocarditis
    • Chagas = T. cruzi
    • Lyme = Borrelia burgdorferi (AV block)
    • Diphtheria = toxin-mediated.
  • Hallmark: focal myocyte necrosis surrounded by inflammatory cells. Dallas criteria: interstitial inflammation + focal myocytic necrosis/degeneration.
  • Gross — severe: softening, flabbiness, pallor, focal hemorrhage, mottled
    • Most instances: enlarged, soft, flabby, dilated chambers, reddish beefy discoloration.
  • Cells:
    • PMNs = bacterial
    • Lymphocytes = viral/autoimmune
    • Eosinophils = hypersensitivity/parasitic.
  • GCM: multinucleated giant cells = sine qua non, extensive necrosis with fragmentation, aggressive, transplant
    • Hypersensitivity: numerous eosinophils + macrophages, no/little necrosis, no granulomas, methyldopa. Acute viral: edema, mononuclear infiltrate, myocyte necrosis, viral inclusions.
  • EMB = gold standard, 4-5 samples from more than one RV site (focal disease).

Valvular, Pericardial, Neoplastic — Must Know Block

Must Know
  • Calcific aortic valve stenosis = most frequent valve abnormality. Heaped calcified masses in cusps, no commissural fusion → concentric LVH, angina, syncope, CHF.
  • Mitral annular calcification: irregular, stony, hard nodules behind the MV leaflets
    • Elderly women.
  • Acute IE: virulent organism, normal valve, destructive bulky friable vegetations
    • Subacute: low virulence (Enterococci, S. viridans), diseased valve, insidious
    • TV in drug mainliners
    • Roth spots.
  • NBTE (marantic): sterile fibrin-platelet thrombi along lines of closure, no inflammation, carcinoma/debilitation/hypercoagulable.
  • Libman-Sacks: SLE, sterile small vegetations on undersurface of cords, hematoxylin bodies
    • Carcinoid: PV and TV, endocardial fibrosis.
  • RF diagnosis: 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor Jones
    • Major: migratory polyarthritis, carditis, subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham's chorea
    • Minor: fever, arthralgia, sore throat/↑ASO, ↑ESR/CRP.
  • ARF morphology: Aschoff bodies, pancarditis, fibrinous pericarditis, verrucal vegetations on lines of closure (MacCallum plaques)
    • CRF: commissural fusion → "fish mouth deformity", chordae shortening/thickening.
  • MVP: most common valvular disease in industrialized countries
    • Hooding/ballooning of leaflets, myxomatous degeneration, midsystolic click. Marfan's.
  • Pericarditis: Serous = RHD, SLE, uremia, viral
    • Fibrinous = most common, "bread and butter" (uremia, RHD, radiation, Dressler)
    • Hemorrhagic = malignant neoplasm spread. Purulent → constrictive pericarditis
    • TB → caseation.
  • Myxoma: most common primary cardiac tumor in adults, 90% LA, fossa ovalis, vessel-like or gland-like structures, ball-valve obstruction, embolization
    • Not malignant.
  • Rhabdomyoma: most frequent primary cardiac tumor in children, ventricles, glycogen removed → "Spider" cells.

Common Confusions / Exam Traps

Exam Traps
  • VSD is the most common CHD overall
    • Secundum ASD is the most common type of ASD. TOF is the most common R-L shunt
    • MVP is the most common valvular disease in industrialized countries
    • Calcific AS is the most frequent valve abnormality.
  • ASD symptoms appear in the 3rd-4th decade. VSD symptoms appear earlier in the pediatric age group.
  • All L-R shunts are acyanotic at birth except AVSD (early cyanosis).
  • Coarctation gives weak lower extremity pulses and upper limb HTN. TOF gives cyanosis, not weak pulses
    • Clubbing is a later manifestation.
  • DCMP = systolic failure, low EF. HCMP = diastolic failure, normal/↑ EF. Both HCMP and amyloid RCMP can show thick walls (amyloid mimics HCMP).
  • DCMP vs HCMP genes: DCMP = cytoskeletal (dystrophin, lamin)
    • HCMP = sarcomere (MYBP-C, β-MHC).
  • HCMP does NOT have eosinophil infiltration
    • HCMP has IVS fiber disorientation, anterior MV leaflet thickening, septal/LV ratio >1.3.
  • Hemochromatosis causes restrictive, not dilated, cardiomyopathy
    • DCMP causes: alcohol, myocarditis, doxorubicin (Adriamycin).
  • Beefy red enlarged heart + interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate with focal necrosis = viral myocarditis. Loeffler's = eosinophilic
    • Fibroelastosis = no inflammation.
  • Subacute IE is less severe than acute IE. Marantic = NBTE. Libman-Sacks (not carcinoid) = SLE. Rheumatic fever = group A strep.
  • Midsystolic click = MVP (myxomatous degeneration), not rheumatic valvulitis (stenosis, no click).
  • Myxoma is benign, not aggressive
    • Caseous pericarditis = TB.
  • Giant cells: sine qua non of GCM. Hypersensitivity myocarditis has no giant cells and no granulomas.

Memory Aids Study aids, derived from lecture wording

  • R-L shunts = the "T's" (stated in the lecture): Tetralogy, Transposition, Truncus, Tricuspid atresia, TAPVR.
  • Tricuspid atresia route: RA → ASD → LA → LV → VSD → RV → Lungs (lecture sequence).
  • DCMP four negatives: no Coronary disease, no Valvular disease, no systemic Hypertension, no Shunts — "CVHS".
  • Lecture descriptors: Dilated = Weak-Flabby, Hypertrophic = Muscle-Bound, Restrictive = Stiff.
  • Serous pericarditis causes: RHD, SLE, Uremia, Viral.
  • Myocarditis cells: PMN = bacterial, Lymphocyte = viral, Eosinophil = parasitic/hypersensitivity (lecture pairing).
  • Coronavirus proteins: Spike binds, Nucleocapsid wraps RNA, Envelope + Membrane form the envelope, M organizes assembly and shape.
